subject: chemistry
question_text: Why is a pressure cooker used for cooking food on hills?

verification.note: Chapter 4 (States of Matter) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.62-66), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The book prints NO Long Answer section for this chapter, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book's model answer stops at water boils at low temperature on hills; this card completes the mechanism (the cooker raises the pressure, which raises the boiling point), because the question asks why the cooker is used.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The problem on hills
lines: At high altitude the atmospheric pressure is low.
A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the
external pressure, so on hills water boils below
100 °C. At this lower temperature food cooks
steps.why: Boiling point is not a fixed property of water; it is set by the external pressure. Lower the external pressure and the boiling point falls with it, and cooking depends on the temperature reached, not on the boiling itself.
common_mistakes: Saying water cannot boil on hills. It boils MORE easily, but at a lower temperature.
Saying the low temperature of hill air is the reason. The reason is the low atmospheric pressure.
steps.memory_tip: Boiling point follows external pressure: low pressure on hills, low boiling temperature.
steps.margin_note: The link boiling point depends on external pressure is the marked idea.

steps.label: What the cooker does
lines: The sealed cooker holds steam, so the pressure
above the water rises above the outside pressure.

lines.text: The higher pressure raises the boiling point, so the food cooks quickly

steps.why: The cooker reverses the altitude problem: trapping steam raises the pressure over the water, the boiling point climbs back above 100 °C, and the food is cooked at a higher temperature in less time.
common_mistakes: Saying the cooker traps heat. The marked point is that it raises the PRESSURE, which raises the boiling temperature.
steps.memory_tip: The cooker is the hill in reverse: more pressure, higher boiling point.
steps.margin_note: Box the pressure-to-boiling-point link; that is the answer to why.

insider_note: Two links make the full answer: low pressure lowers the boiling point, and the cooker raises the pressure back. Most students write only the first and lose the second mark.
